title: Locally Picked, LLC produce and honey seller: accrual vs. cash basis accounting, accounts receivable and payable, three disputed June entries
participant_role: Associate accountant hired by the owner of LOCALLY PICKED, LLC to explain accrual basis accounting
judge_role: Owner of LOCALLY PICKED, LLC, a small farmer's market business that has always used cash basis accounting
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an associate accountant hired by the owner (judge) of LOCALLY PICKED, LLC., a small business that sells fresh locally grown fruits, vegetables, and honey. The owner (judge) needs you to explain accrual basis accounting.

LOCALLY PICKED, LLC is growing and has started selling its items to larger grocery chains in the region. As a small farmer's market, the owner (judge) had always used cash basis accounting. The owner (judge) was recently told that they should be using accrual basis accounting and does not understand the reason.

The owner (judge) has been selling fruits, vegetable and honey to the grocery store chain and billing the store. The owner (judge) was told that revenue must be recorded at the time of the sale, but the owner (judge) feels that does not make sense since revenue has not been received because cash has not been received. The owner (judge) needs your help understanding this concept and why accrual basis accounting is the preferred method.

The owner (judge) has listed three transactions that are in dispute:
- June 10th, sold fruits, vegetables, and honey to the grocery store for $1,000 and billed the grocery store with terms 2/10, n/30.
- June 20th purchased a refrigerator for $2,000, did not pay at the time of purchase, was billed for it, and will pay for it in July.
- June 30th prepaid liability insurance for $3,000 that covers the last six months of the year.

You are to meet with the owner (judge) to:
- Explain how accrual basis accounting works and why it is preferred over cash basis accounting.
- Discuss the definition of accounts receivable and accounts payable.
- Go over the three transactions above and demonstrate how they should be recorded under accrual basis accounting.

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Explain how accrual basis accounting works and why it is preferred over cash basis accounting
Discuss the definition of accounts receivable and accounts payable
Go over the three transactions above and demonstrate how they should be recorded under accrual basis accounting

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned (when produce is delivered to the grocery store) and expenses when incurred or when an asset is used, so profit for a period is measured correctly, which cash basis cannot do. It defines accounts receivable (asset, what customers owe, debit to increase) and accounts payable (liability, what the business owes vendors, credit to increase), then journalizes the three June transactions: Accounts Receivable/Sales $1,000, Refrigerator/Accounts Payable $2,000, Prepaid Insurance/Cash $3,000, and explains the follow-up entries.

by_task.task: How accrual accounting works and why it is preferred
answer: Accrual basis: revenue is recorded when earned, so when the fruits, vegetables and honey are delivered to the grocery store the sale is recognized even though cash has not arrived
Expenses are recorded when incurred or when an asset is used up, not when the bill is paid
This matches the expenses that were required to generate the revenue in the same period, so the owner can see the true profit for each month or year
Cash basis records only when cash moves, so revenue and the related expenses can land in different periods and profit for a period may be wrong
GAAP (accounting standards) requires accrual accounting, and larger customers, lenders and the IRS (once the business grows) expect it
Accounts receivable tracks how much all customers owe you, such as the grocery chain's $1,000 bill; it is an asset on the balance sheet
Accounts receivable increases with a debit and decreases with a credit when the customer pays
Accounts payable tracks how much you owe all vendors, such as the $2,000 refrigerator bill; it is a liability on the balance sheet
Accounts payable increases with a credit and decreases with a debit when you pay
Both accounts are used when buying and selling on trade credit
June 10: debit Accounts Receivable 1,000, credit Sales 1,000; revenue is recognized on delivery even though the store has not paid

Terms 2/10, n/30 mean the store may deduct 2% ($20) if it pays within 10 days, otherwise the full $1,000 is due in 30 days; if paid early, debit Cash 980 and Sales Discounts 20, credit Accounts Receivable 1,000
June 20: debit Refrigerator (Equipment) 2,000, credit Accounts Payable 2,000; the refrigerator is a long-term asset, not an expense, and the debt is recorded now even though payment is in July

June 30: debit Prepaid Insurance 3,000, credit Cash 3,000; the payment buys six months of coverage, so it is an asset that becomes expense at $500 per month (debit Insurance Expense 500, credit Prepaid Insurance 500 each month July through December)
Under cash basis the owner would have shown no June sale, no refrigerator debt and a $3,000 June expense, which distorts June's profit

judge_question_answers.question: How should expenses for bottling honey be classified?
answer: Bottling costs (jars, lids, labels, labor to fill them) are product costs: they become part of the inventory cost of the honey and are recorded as Cost of Goods Sold when the honey is sold
Under accrual accounting they are matched to the revenue from the honey sale, not expensed when the jars are bought
If the amounts are small, a simpler approach is a Packaging Supplies expense account, but keep it separate from selling and administrative expenses so gross profit on honey is visible

judge_question_answers.question: How can I tell if my business is doing well?
answer: Prepare an income statement each month under accrual accounting and check that net income (revenue minus expenses) is positive and growing
Watch the balance sheet: accounts receivable being collected on time, accounts payable paid on time and cash on hand to cover bills
Track ratios such as gross profit margin and net profit margin (net income / sales) and compare them month to month and to similar businesses
Compare actual results to a budget and to last year to spot trends

key_concepts.definition: Recording revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands; required by GAAP.
Recording revenue only when cash is received and expenses only when cash is paid; simple but can misstate profit for a period.
Revenue is recorded when earned, which for goods is when they are delivered to the customer, even if the customer has not paid.
Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped produce so profit for the period is measured correctly.
An asset account tracking what customers owe the business; increases with a debit, decreases with a credit when collected.
A liability account tracking what the business owes its vendors; increases with a credit, decreases with a debit when paid.
The buyer may take a 2% discount if it pays within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days.
A payment made in advance for a future benefit, such as six months of insurance; recorded as an asset and moved to expense as it is used (3,000 / 6 = 500 per month).
An end-of-period entry that updates accounts under accrual accounting, such as expensing one month of prepaid insurance.
A long-lived item like a refrigerator that is recorded as an asset when bought and depreciated over its useful life, rather than expensed.
The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time (accounts receivable and payable live here); the income statement shows revenue, expenses and net income for a period.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the standards that require accrual accounting so financial statements are consistent and comparable.
